title: Mass extinctions
what: The great mass extinctions, where their causes and records lay at the time, and what the studies say caused each.
how: Each extinction is marked within 5 million years of its time: where its cause lay, or a cause held or argued (the Siberian, Emeishan, Deccan and Viluy Traps, the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province, Chicxulub, the Hirnantian ice sheet’s deposits in the Sahara), and where it is dated (the boundary’s reference section), with other sections that record it: the end-Permian on land in the Karoo and the Sydney Basin, the end-Triassic at St Audrie’s Bay, the end-Cretaceous’s iridium at Gubbio, the Hirnantian’s base at Wangjiawan. The places are approximate, compiled for this site, and carried back on the PALEOMAP model by the GPlates Web Service. Each card also gives where Merdith et al.’s model puts the place at its extinction, and how far the two disagree: ancient latitudes are fixed by the rocks’ magnetism, longitudes are not, so models differ most in those. Dates are the milestones’, with their sources. The list itself is argued: the usual five are Raup & Sepkoski’s, Bambach finds only three stand apart, and Rampino & Shen put the end-Guadalupian forward as a sixth, shown here as argued. Where the causes are argued, the card gives each side. Bond & Grasby’s review ties most great extinctions to large igneous provinces. Chicxulub and the end-Permian can be watched in their own time, Chicxulub’s strike with the Deccan Traps fuming beside it through its million years, steady and pale, since both readings have them erupting then and which came first is what is argued: deep time hands over to their clock as it plays past them at Slow, and offers it faster. The end-Permian’s clock counts from the extinction’s start at Meishan, linearly across the crisis from 400,000 years before to 200,000 after, then by tenfolds to 10 million years after, each phase from the studies that place it. The end-Triassic and the end-Guadalupian can be watched on the same clock, the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province and the Emeishan Traps fuming; the end-Triassic’s four pulses are spread evenly over their 600,000 years, an assumption. The end-Ordovician and the Late Devonian run on a longer clock, a million years before their first pulse to two million after: the Ordovician’s ice sheet growing to its maximum and melting, and oxygen-poor water spreading in patches round the places their records come from, over the sea only, as the deep-time heights draw it, darkest over the shallow shelves, the Kellwasser pulses drawn 150,000 years long, an assumption. Under the fumes, lava fountains at the vents, and the flood lavas spreading over the land as far as each province had erupted by then: the Siberian Traps two thirds before and during the extinction, the Central Atlantic province a quarter with each pulse, the Emeishan Traps mostly in their first million years (how it was spread drawn, not measured), and the Deccan held at half, since before or after the impact is argued; glowing at the flood’s outer front and by the vents while it erupts, dark basalt behind. The fumes, the lava, the ice and the patches are illustrations, not a model: plumes from vents spread over the traps, pale over the flood lavas and dark with the sills’ gas, as strong as the phases say, and a haze over the globe; their heights and sizes are drawn to be seen.
